questions.prompt: An investor ranks the four listed companies by which name feels most familiar. What is the main mistake?
choices: Familiarity should be used before price because recognition proves value.
Price must be compared with the record because reputation alone can hide what is being paid for earnings and assets.
A familiar name should be avoided because recognition always signals overvaluation.
questions.explanation: Recognition is not valuation. The four-company method compares price with record rather than reputation alone.

questions.prompt: Emerson Electric looks like the strongest business in a comparison. What should still be checked before buying?
choices: Whether the company is famous enough to ignore valuation.
Whether business quality removes the effect of a premium price.
Whether the price already reflects high expectations and reduces future return.
questions.explanation: A high-quality business can still require valuation caution. Investment result depends on price as well as quality.

questions.prompt: A growth-company comparison shows strong growth reputation and a high multiple. What question disciplines the judgment?
choices: How much of the growth is already capitalized in the price?
Whether growth reputation alone makes the company cheap.
Whether disappointment is irrelevant when growth has been strong.
questions.explanation: Growth can be overpaid for. High multiples can leave little room for disappointment if expectations are already capitalized.

questions.prompt: Two companies show appealing income statement growth, but one relies more heavily on debt. What should change in the comparison?
choices: Debt should be ignored because growth alone ranks the companies.
The company with more debt should automatically rank higher because leverage increases earnings.
Balance-sheet strength should be weighed because leverage changes downside risk and the value of earnings.
questions.explanation: Balance-sheet strength affects the comparison. Debt can make growth fragile and change how earnings should be valued.

questions.prompt: A comparison shows reported prosperity, but the dividend record is being dismissed as irrelevant. What is being missed?
choices: Cash distributions are a cross-check on whether earnings reached shareholders.
Dividends settle every valuation question without looking at price.
Dividend records matter only when earnings are ignored.
questions.explanation: Dividend record supplies one visible test of financial maturity because cash distributions show whether earnings reached shareholders.

questions.prompt: A lower-quality company appears beside a stronger one, but its price is much lower relative to its prospects. What conclusion fits disciplined comparison?
choices: The lower-quality company must be rejected because quality rankings and investment rankings are identical.
The lower-quality company may be more attractive if valuation compensates for weaker prospects within limits.
The strongest company must rank first regardless of price.
questions.explanation: Price can reverse the order. A lower-quality company may be more attractive when valuation compensates for weaker prospects within limits.

questions.prompt: An investor wants to settle the ranking from one annual report because the latest comparison looks clear. What is the problem?
choices: Cyclical or temporary conditions can distort apparent standing, so multi-year records are needed.
One annual report is enough when the narrative is compelling.
Multi-year records should be avoided because they weaken recent evidence.
questions.explanation: A single comparison year is not enough. Temporary or cyclical conditions can distort how each company appears.

questions.prompt: Emerson Electric and Emery Air Freight both report earnings, but their businesses have different capital needs and margins. What should the comparison avoid?
choices: Treating industry context as relevant to capitalization.
Giving all earnings dollars the same multiple without considering business economics.
Comparing companies from different businesses at all.
questions.explanation: Industry context matters because capital needs and margins differ across industrial, electrical, and freight businesses. Business economics change capitalization.

questions.prompt: A compelling company story conflicts with a side-by-side table showing unfavorable ratios. What should carry more weight?
choices: The narrative, because a single story is clearer than multiple facts.
The story, as long as the ratios are inconvenient rather than favorable.
The side-by-side evidence, because tables force multiple facts into view at once.
questions.explanation: Side-by-side tables discipline judgment. Narratives can hide unfavorable ratios, while tables force several facts to be confronted together.

cards.front: What does the four-company method compare instead of reputation alone?
cards.back: It compares price with record. Names and narratives can obscure what the buyer is paying for earnings and assets.

cards.front: Why can Emerson Electric still require valuation caution?
cards.back: A high-quality business can be priced so richly that future return is reduced. Investment result depends on price as well as quality.

cards.front: What must a growth-company comparison ask?
cards.back: It must ask how much growth is already capitalized. High multiples can leave little room for disappointment.

cards.front: Why does balance-sheet strength affect a company comparison?
cards.back: Leverage changes both downside risk and the value of earnings. Debt can make growth fragile.
It checks whether reported prosperity has reached shareholders through cash distributions. Dividends are one visible test of financial maturity.

cards.back: A lower-quality company may be more attractive if its valuation sufficiently compensates for weaker prospects within limits.
